content: The criteria documents serve as the scientific foundation for establishing new occupational safety and health standards. These documents typically include a comprehensive review of the scientific and technical data available regarding the prevalence of hazards, the existence of safety and health risks, and the effectiveness of control measures. In addition to submitting these documents to the Department of Labor, the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) also distributes them to health professionals in academic institutions, industries, labor organizations, public interest groups, and other government agencies. This specific criteria document evaluates the available information on the adverse health effects associated with exposure to ethylene glycol monobutyl ether (EGBE) and ethylene glycol monobutyl ether acetate (EGBEA). Animal studies have demonstrated clear, dose-dependent adverse effects on the central nervous system, hematopoietic tissues, blood, kidneys, and liver across multiple species via various routes of administration. Limited human data also suggest risks of adverse effects on the central nervous system, hematopoietic tissues, blood, and kidneys. Due to the scarcity of human data, NIOSH bases its recommended exposure limits (RELs) for EGBE and EGBEA on animal study data, adjusted to account for uncertainties in extrapolating findings from animals to humans. NIOSH assumes full responsibility for the conclusions and recommendations presented in this document. NIOSH recommends that worker exposure to EGBE and EGBEA in the workplace be controlled in accordance with the provisions outlined in Chapter 1 of this document. These recommendations are designed to protect workers' health and ensure their safety during a 10-hour work shift and a 40-hour workweek over a working lifetime. Adherence to these recommendations should prevent or significantly reduce the risk of adverse effects among exposed workers. However, because environmental contaminant concentrations can vary daily, a time-weighted average (TWA) exposure below the REL on a given day does not guarantee that exposures on other days will also remain below the REL. If a worker's TWA exposure during a work shift is at or above half the REL, it is likely that exposures will exceed the REL on other days. Therefore, an action level of half the REL should be adopted to ensure adequate worker protection. Recommended Exposure Limits for EGBE and EGBEA Worker exposure to EGBE and EGBEA in the workplace must be controlled to ensure that concentrations do not exceed 5 parts per million (ppm) of air (24 mg EGBE/m³ or 33 mg EGBEA/m³). Dermal contact must be prohibited because EGBE and EGBEA are readily absorbed through the skin. Sampling and Analysis Workplace air samples for EGBE should be collected and analyzed as described in the NIOSH Manual of Analytical Methods, Method No. 1403, which can also be adapted for EGBEA. OSHA Method No. 83 is also recommended for sampling and analysis of EGBE and EGBEA. The action level in this standard is the concentration at which exposure monitoring and medical monitoring should begin. Industrial Hygiene Surveys Employers must conduct initial industrial hygiene surveys in work areas where airborne exposures to EGBE or EGBEA may occur. These surveys should determine exposure levels using personal sampling techniques over an entire work shift. Records of these surveys must be maintained. If exposures are determined to be below the REL, the records must document the basis for this conclusion. Surveys must be repeated at least annually and whenever process changes are likely to increase airborne concentrations of EGBE or EGBEA. Employers must also evaluate and document the potential for skin exposure. Personal monitoring samples representative of TWA exposures to airborne EGBE and EGBEA must be collected in the worker's breathing zone. Sufficient samples must be collected to characterize the exposure of all workers, considering variations in work schedules, production processes, and job functions. If a worker is exposed to EGBE or EGBEA below the REL but at or above the action level, exposure monitoring must occur at least every six months or as otherwise indicated by a professional industrial hygienist. If exposure exceeds the REL, the worker must wear a respirator until adequate engineering controls or work practices are implemented. Controls must then be initiated, the worker must be notified of the exposure and control measures, and weekly exposure evaluations must be conducted until two consecutive determinations at least one week apart indicate that exposure no longer exceeds the REL. At that point, semiannual monitoring should be instituted. If concentrations below the action level are noted after two consecutive semiannual surveys, sampling can be conducted annually. Medical Monitoring Employers must provide the following information to the physician responsible for the medical monitoring program: The requirements of the applicable standard. An estimate of the worker's potential exposure to EGBE or EGBEA, including any workplace sampling results. A description of the worker's duties related to exposure. A description of any protective equipment the worker may be required to use. Employers must establish a medical monitoring program for all workers exposed to airborne concentrations of EGBE or EGBEA at or above the action level or with potential for skin exposure. Medical examinations and procedures must be performed by or under the direction of a licensed physician and provided without cost to the worker. These examinations should focus on the blood, hematopoietic and central nervous systems, skin, liver, and kidneys. Periodic medical examinations must be provided at least annually for all workers occupationally exposed to EGBE or EGBEA at or above the action level or with potential for skin exposure. Labeling and Posting All labels and warning signs must be printed in English and the predominant language of workers who do not read English. Workers unable to read the labels and signs must be verbally informed of the instructions. Containers of EGBE or EGBEA used or stored in the workplace must carry a permanently attached, visible label identifying the glycol ether and providing information on its health effects and emergency procedures. Warning signs must be posted in visible locations in work areas where exposures may exceed the REL or where skin exposure may occur. Protective Clothing and Equipment Engineering controls and good work practices must be used to maintain airborne concentrations of EGBE and EGBEA below the REL and prevent skin and eye contact. When protective clothing and equipment are necessary, they must be provided by the employer. Workers at risk of skin exposure must be provided with appropriate protective clothing, such as gloves and disposable garments. Contaminated clothing must be cleaned before reuse, and those handling such clothing must be informed of the hazards and proper precautions. Respiratory Protection Engineering controls and good work practices should be the primary methods for controlling respiratory exposure to airborne contaminants. Respirators should only be used as a secondary measure during specific situations, such as implementing engineering controls, short-duration maintenance, or emergencies. Employers must ensure that respirators are properly fitted and that workers are trained annually in their use and testing for leakage. Workers must not be assigned tasks requiring respirators unless they are physically able to perform the work and use the equipment. Emergency Procedures Emergency plans and procedures must be developed for all work areas where exposure to EGBE or EGBEA is possible. Workers must be trained in the effective implementation of these plans. In the event of a leak or spill, nonessential personnel must be evacuated, ignition sources removed, and the area ventilated. Spilled material must be contained and absorbed with appropriate materials, and contaminated absorbents must be disposed of as hazardous waste. Storage and Waste Disposal EGBE and EGBEA must be stored in cool, well-ventilated areas away from acids, bases, and oxidizing agents. Waste materials must be securely packaged, labeled, and incinerated. Food, beverages, cosmetics, and tobacco products must not be stored or used in areas where EGBE or EGBEA is produced or used. Training Employers must implement a continuing education program to ensure that all workers exposed to EGBE or EGBEA are knowledgeable about the hazards, proper maintenance, cleanup methods, and use of protective equipment. Workers must also be trained in emergency and evacuation procedures. Ventilation and Work Practices Local exhaust ventilation systems must be designed to prevent the accumulation of airborne EGBE or EGBEA. Systems must be regularly inspected and maintained to ensure effectiveness. Confined spaces must be ventilated and tested for oxygen deficiency and airborne concentrations before entry. Emergency procedures must be in place to address leaks, spills, and other incidents.
